narrative:
The model predicted a 72.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to decide offers, your application was rejected.

The strongest reason for this outcome was your first-year and third-year class rankings. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked around the middle of their class. These two factors were the most influential in the decision and pushed strongly toward predicting failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5, which is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, worked in the opposite direction and helped the model somewhat, but it was not enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 38, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time were all close to or better than typical accepted students, yet they carried less weight in the final prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing in law school so that your class rank improves significantly. Consider targeted bar-prep programs, practice exams, or academic support services that directly address performance in the core curriculum. Reapplying with a stronger record of consistent high performance could change the outcome. (218 words)
